newsitem.title: PERU: Peru hostage crisis seen coming close to an end.
newsitem.headline: Peru hostage crisis seen coming close to an end.

text.p: One hundred days after Marxist rebels stormed the Japanese ambassador's home in Lima taking hundreds of hostages, there is a sense of optimism that a negotiated solution may be in sight.
Such is the mood that even President Alberto Fujimori's opponents in Congress see a quick end to the crisis.
"The way negotiations are progressing, I believe they can come up with a solution in the short term," Congressman Alejandro Santa Maria Silva of the Aprista party told Reuters.

The wave of optimism among diplomats and politicians this week was reinforced on Thursday by comments from Fujimori and the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels who are holding 72 hostages at the residence in plush San Isidro.
"Even though, naturally, difficulties still exist, we are getting closer," Fujimori told a television interviewer.

An MRTA military leader in Peru's central jungle agreed there was progress but said the government still had to come up with a satisfactory offer to meet the rebels' demand for the freedom of jailed comrades. "The sides are getting closer but the main demand for the release of prisoners still has to be addressed," Comrade Alejandro told Reuters from the jungle.

Diplomats, legislators and analysts all say that, although they foresee tough discussions on how many, if any, of the 450 MRTA imprisoned rebels would be released, that should not become an unsurmountable hurdle when face-to-face contacts resume, presumably early next week after the Easter holiday.

A three-man "guarantors commission" of Canada's Ambassador Anthony Vincent, Red Cross representative Michel Minning and Archbishop Juan Cipriani has kept the sides in touch but there has not been a face-to-face dialogue for more than two weeks.
Once they get together, talks could go into high gear.

Analysts cite two other elements to justify their optimism -- political asylum offered by Cuba and the Dominican Republic for the 20-odd rebels holed up in the residence and the MRTA's success in attracting the world's attention to their cause.

"Politically, they have gained a lot," analyst Carlos Perez said. "They have become the main actors in Peru's political scenario in the last three months, and they have put the government in a tight spot."

That could have the sweet taste of revenge for a group that suffered a series of devastating military defeats since Fujimori first came to power in 1990. Some 1,000 foreign journalists including all major Japanese TV and newspapers have given the MRTA international exposure like never before.

The 72 male captives include Japan's ambassador Morihisa Aoki and about two dozen other Japanese nationals, mostly businessmen. They were attending a cocktail party at the residence on Dec. 17 when the rebels blasted their way in and took more than 500 hostages, most of whom were later released.
Experts say the media attention, an MRTA public relations coup, could be behind their reported inclination to tone down initial demands for the release of all their comrades.

Carlos Tapia, an independent analyst, suggested MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini could capitalise on the publicity and even try to run for Congress. "He has won international recognition now. Why should he go back to the jungle and get himself killed along with a few kids?"
On the other hand, Fujimori could also claim victory, showing he could handle a major crisis without a bloodbath and without caving in to the rebels' demands for the release of all 450 prisoners.

Amid the optimism, one former hostage who asked not to be identified urged caution. He pointed out that having dozens of captives under the guns of hardened rebels was far from a calm scenario. "The situation is very fragile," he said.
